comments.content: The `reject` filter now only excludes `$qualifiedKeyName` but no longer excludes `$keyName`. If the original query orders by the unqualified key name (e.g. `orderBy('id')`), it will not be rejected here, but the later `distinct($qualifiedKeyName)` check on line 154 compares against both `$keyName` and `$qualifiedKeyName`. This asymmetry can lead to inconsistent handling. Consider keeping both `[$keyName, $qualifiedKeyName]` in the reject list, or documenting why only the qualified name should be rejected.

`$originalOrders` is a Collection built with `unique('column')`, so its keys are not guaranteed to be sequential starting at 0. Accessing `$originalOrders[0]` and calling `$originalOrders->forget(0)` assumes index 0 exists and is the first element. If the first order was de-duplicated or filtered out, key `0` may not exist, causing an undefined index. Use `$originalOrders->first()` and `$originalOrders->shift()` (or reset keys via `->values()`) to safely obtain and remove the first element.

This reads `$query->getQuery()->orders[0]` directly, but after the `reorder(...)` calls above, the orders array is rebuilt. Ensure `orders` is non-empty before indexing `[0]`; if the query has no orders at this point, `orders[0]` yields null and `distinct($qualifiedKeyName)` is skipped, which may unintentionally drop the distinct behavior needed for stable chunking. Verify this branch handles the empty-orders case correctly.
